item.title: China's "importathon" at nine -- what keeps it running?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
SHANGHAI, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- Thousands of overseas businesses are gearing up to meet buyers in Shanghai in east China at a trade fair devoted to imports. The draw is China, the world's second-largest import market. The occasion is the ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE), set to be held from Nov. 5 to 10 at the four-leaf-clover-shaped National Exhibition and Convention Center (Shanghai). Its 4,142 overseas exhibitors include more than 2,000 newcomers alongside veterans of every previous edition. Call it an "importathon" -- a blend of "import" and "marathon." Announced in 2017 and held annually since 2018, the CIIE has become a fixture on the global trade calendar, helping China expand imports and open its massive market wider to the world. But what keeps the event running, and why do businesses keep returning? CHINA MEANS BUSINESS ON IMPORTS In May 2017, China announced plans for a trade fair with a different focus: imports rather than exports. When the first CIIE opened in Shanghai the following year, it became the world's first national-level expo dedicated to imports, forming part of China's drive to open its market wider and support an open world economy. China has since described the CIIE as a showcase of its new development paradigm, a platform for high-standard opening-up and a public good for the whole world. The idea is simple: businesses worldwide can share in the opportunities offered by China's market. Imports also serve China's own development needs. Imported consumer goods give households more choice, while advanced equipment and technologies can support industrial upgrading. Greater imports of goods and services can also help meet domestic demand and promote more balanced trade. This push continues in 2026, the first year of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). This year's government work report calls for boosting imports to promote balanced trade. The five-year blueprint also calls for expanded imports of advanced technology and equipment, quality agricultural products, and producer services to meet domestic needs. The blueprint explicitly calls for continuing to hold the CIIE and other major trade fairs, including the Canton Fair in south China, while strengthening trade-promotion platforms. THE RETURN ON RETURNING Roughly half of this year's exhibitors are returning, but they occupy around 80 percent of the exhibition space. Among them are 169 companies and 30 overseas exhibition organizers back for a ninth consecutive edition. One such stalwart is French yeast maker Lesaffre. In a written interview with Xinhua, its Greater China president, Jerome Vanachter, described the CIIE as a "market-intelligence hub" that helps turn market insights into products. The CIIE does more than showcase products. It brings policymakers, researchers, entrepreneurs and businesses together, creating opportunities for trade, investment and joint innovation. Such connections start before the doors open. Trade matchmaking sessions have already been held in countries including Egypt, Germany and Britain. More than 40 trade delegations and over 600 sub-delegations are expected at the expo, while the "CIIE Goes Local" initiative extends matchmaking to provinces and cities across China. These connections need not end when the fair closes. The 2025 CIIE recorded 83.49 billion U.S. dollars in intended deals for purchases over one year. Shanghai has also developed a "six days plus 365 days" approach to year-round trading. As of July 2026, Hongqiao 365, a CIIE-linked trading platform, featured more than 85,000 products from over 120 countries and regions, about 70 percent of them previously exhibited at the expo. For Danish pump maker Grundfos, it all started with a small display board in the Danish pavilion at the inaugural CIIE. The company later returned as an independent exhibitor. After the fourth edition, it announced an investment of roughly 100 million U.S. dollars in a new factory in Changshu, east China's Jiangsu Province. The plant opened in 2024. Bent Jensen, a Grundfos executive, said the expo helps the company better understand Chinese market demand and connect with clients across Asia and other global partners. INNOVATION GOES BOTH WAYS For international companies, the CIIE doubles as a testing ground for new ideas. Product launches put new offerings directly in front of Chinese buyers, giving companies a chance to gauge demand and find local development or production partners. This is one expression of China's "debut economy," which links product debuts with research, production and sales. More than 3,400 new products, technologies and services debuted during the first eight editions of the CIIE. This year, over 480 exhibits are set to make their global, Asian or China debuts -- a record for the event. Shanghai Vice Mayor Lu Shan has said that feedback from such launches strengthens exhibitors' confidence in investing in China. Some have since established production operations or research hubs in China serving global markets. For some multinationals, China's appeal lies not just in its customers but also in opportunities to innovate together, a shift some call "China Opportunity 2.0." "At the CIIE, we sit down with Chinese partners and explore how we can innovate together," Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said. The German life sciences giant plans to showcase nearly 30 innovations making their CIIE debut. Michelin shows how technology can move from the show floor to the market. The French tire maker displayed Formula E racing-tire technology at the 2020 CIIE, then brought it to the Chinese market in May 2021 following interest from local automakers and consumers. This year, the company plans an Asian debut for its tire digital-twin solution, which uses vehicle data to help monitor tire performance. Innovation can flow outward as well. Through its BIG BANG beauty-tech collaboration program, L'Oréal worked with Nanomed, a company based in Suzhou in east China, to develop a Lancome skincare device. Displayed at the 2025 CIIE, this device was on sale in more than 20 countries and regions by July 2026. OPENING UP IN PRACTICE "This expo matters because it opens doors," Rebeca Grynspan, secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, said in a video address to the 2025 CIIE opening ceremony. The fair is one prominent example of China's efforts to make its domestic market more accessible to overseas businesses. The opening-up drive extends beyond the exhibition halls. In November 2024, China removed the last two manufacturing-related restrictions from its national negative list for foreign investment. In January 2026, meanwhile, Chinese authorities said nine additional cities would implement 159 pilot measures to further open the services sector. On Dec. 18, 2025, China launched island-wide special customs operations in the Hainan Free Trade Port in south China, expanding the share of tariff lines eligible for zero-tariff treatment on qualifying imports from 21 percent to 74 percent. Goods shipped onward from Hainan to the Chinese mainland remain subject to separate customs controls. Since May 1, 2026, China has extended zero-tariff treatment to eligible goods from all 53 African countries with which it maintains diplomatic relations. This year's CIIE will feature an upgraded Asia-Africa products zone to help African countries capitalize on the policy, while expanding free exhibition space for the least developed countries by 17 percent. Gao Lingyun, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, described "China Opportunity 2.0" as part of a new wave of industrial transformation -- not about displacing others, but about working together to "make the pie bigger" and helping more developing countries benefit from technological progress. As the ninth edition approaches, the "importathon" again promises more than six days of exhibitions. Its appeal lies in the chance to turn a debut into a sale, a business meeting into an investment, and market access into lasting partnerships. ■

item.title: From ancient wisdom to modern engineering: How China manages the Yellow River
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
From an ancient vision to modern engineering, China is using precisely controlled water and sediment regulation to tackle sediment buildup in its mother river, the Yellow River. Through 33 coordinated reservoir operations, the average riverbed elevation of the main channel in the lower reaches has been reduced by 3.1 meters, helping improve the river's long-term health and flood prevention.■

item.title: Body of former Chinese vice premier Liu Yandong cremated
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
Xi Jinping shakes hands with a family member of Liu Yandong to express deep condolences in Beijing, capital of China, Nov. 3, 2026. The body of Liu Yandong, a former Chinese vice premier and state councilor, was cremated in Beijing on Tuesday. President Xi Jinping and other senior leaders of the Communist Party of China and the state, including Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi and Han Zheng, bid Liu farewell at the Babaoshan Revolutionary Cemetery on Tuesday morning. (Xinhua/Xie Huanchi) BEIJING, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- The body of Liu Yandong, a former Chinese vice premier and state councilor, was cremated in Beijing on Tuesday. She died of illness in Beijing on Oct. 28 at the age of 81. President Xi Jinping and other senior leaders of the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the state, including Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi and Han Zheng, bid Liu farewell at the Babaoshan Revolutionary Cemetery on Tuesday morning. Amid mournful strains of funeral music, they stood in silent tribute before Liu's remains and paid their final respects with three bows. They shook hands with Liu's family members to offer their condolences. Liu had also served as a member of the Political Bureau of the 17th and 18th CPC Central Committees, and as vice chairperson of the 10th National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, China's top political advisory body. She was extolled as an excellent Party member, a time-tested and loyal communist fighter, and an outstanding leader in the CPC's united front work and in the fields of education, science and technology, health, and work for women and children in China. Xi Jinping, Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi, Han Zheng and Hu Jintao, among others, had either visited Liu while she was in the hospital or expressed deep condolences over her passing and offered sincere sympathies to her family members through various means. ■

item.title: Feature: U.S. voters head to polls in high-stakes midterm elections
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
by Xinhua writers Shi Chun, Xu Jianmei, Liu Yanan NEW YORK, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- American voters are heading to the polls on Tuesday in high-stakes midterm elections, with dissatisfaction over the economy, the war with Iran and deepening political divisions looming large in the closely watched elections. The elections come as the United States grapples with persistent inflation and soaring fuel prices, while concerns over immigration and government corruption add to public frustration. John Heinzinger, 59, a building design contractor in Chicago, told Xinhua that high prices for gasoline, diesel and groceries were weighing on everyday Americans, largely because of the Iran war. "As long as the war is going on, we're not going to see the energy crisis reduced," he said. Heinzinger, a registered Republican voter, expressed frustration that the war and economic pressures had weakened the party's base, but said he continued to support the GOP because of its border control policy. "The price of gas is at crazy all-time highs right now, and that's almost exclusively because of the war that we're fighting for basically no reason," said William Reese, a student at the Georgia Institute of Technology, outside a polling station in Atlanta. Reese said what he described as blatant abuses of power and government corruption over the past two years had damaged the country in both the short and long term, undermining the prospects of ordinary people trying to make ends meet and build a better future. "People are desperate for a change," he said. For Nick Scholefield, a 32-year-old musician with the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra, ending the war with Iran is one of the most pressing issues. "Stop making the United States seem like such a bully on the international stage. It's just a bad look for the country," he said. About three in four American voters are dissatisfied with the U.S. economy, according to the NBC News poll released Sunday. The survey also found that 70 percent believe the country is headed in the wrong direction, up 9 percentage points from a year ago. For many voters, the midterm elections offer an opportunity to voice their dissatisfaction and push for a change in the country's political direction. "I think most people would say the country is not being led in the right direction," said Allan Jennings, a lawyer in New York. "People are suffering from high fuel prices and food prices, so they want change." Shannon Lane, 51, a network safety expert from Chattanooga, Tennessee, said he hoped the country could move beyond its bitter political divisions. "We need to get back to a place where we learn how to talk to each other again, where we can reach consensus on things, where we're not being held hostage by a rhetoric of hate," he said. What kind of change the midterm elections will bring, however, remains uncertain. While some voters see the elections as a chance to reshape the country's political landscape, others are skeptical that the outcome will make much difference. "I think a lot of people are really fed up with the way that the current administration is acting, and making their voices heard with these votes. And I think that, in some way or another, this country will look very different after these midterm elections," Reese said. Summer Whitlock, a voter from Fort Payne, Alabama, was not so optimistic, saying she did not believe the election results would make a difference. Regardless of whether Democrats or Republicans win, "it's going to be corrupt either way," she said. ■

item.title: Global partners share biodiversity, green development views in giant panda hometown
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
The Global Panda Partners Conference 2026 is launched in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, Nov. 3, 2026. The main forum of the Global Panda Partners Conference 2026 opened on Tuesday in southwest China's Sichuan Province, known as the "hometown of giant pandas," drawing experts and scholars from over 30 countries and regions. Under the theme of protecting giant panda habitats, building a beautiful world and sharing open opportunities, the event, being held in Chengdu, the provincial capital, has gathered global guests to discuss biopersity conservation and green development cooperation. (Xinhua/Xu Bingjie) CHENGDU, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- The main forum of the Global Panda Partners Conference 2026 opened on Tuesday in southwest China's Sichuan Province, known as the "hometown of giant pandas," drawing experts and scholars from over 30 countries and regions. Under the theme of protecting giant panda habitats, building a beautiful world and sharing open opportunities, the event, being held in Chengdu, the provincial capital, has gathered global guests to discuss biodiversity conservation and green development cooperation. The main forum also saw the release of a think tank report centered on China's green development path. In her speech, Shi Xiaolin, the province's governor, said Sichuan serves as a vital water conservation zone in the upper reaches of the Yangtze River, a key replenishment area in the upper reaches of the Yellow River, and a globally significant region for biodiversity conservation. The province is firmly committed to the path of giving priority to ecological conservation and pursuing green development, she added. Lyu Yansong, editor-in-chief of Xinhua News Agency, said giant pandas are China's national treasure and a shared wealth of all humanity. He noted that the Global Panda Partners Conference is striving to become an important bond for gathering global wisdom and jointly protecting the planet, while continuously expanding the circle of friends of "panda partners." According to Li Yunqing, deputy head of the National Forestry and Grassland Administration, the captive population of giant pandas in China has reached 830, while the genetic diversity of the population continues to improve. Noting that this year marks the 30th anniversary of international scientific research cooperation on giant pandas, the official said that China has cooperated with 26 institutions in 20 countries, resulting in 69 giant pandas living overseas and 73 cubs successfully bred, while the species has drawn over 1 billion visits worldwide. Shahbaz Khan, director of the UNESCO Regional Office for East Asia, said the giant panda inspires affection across languages and generations, and protecting this remarkable animal means caring for the living systems that sustain many other species and support human well-being. China's establishment of the Giant Panda National Park in 2021 has provided an important framework for conservation across the provinces of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu. Work to restore habitats, reconnect ecological corridors and strengthen coordinated management offers valuable experience in protecting ecosystems across administrative boundaries, he noted. "UNESCO looks forward to continued dialogue with Chinese and international partners on safeguarding natural heritage," the director said. Running from Monday to Wednesday, the conference features a main forum, multiple parallel sessions, and other supporting activities centered on international cooperation in giant panda conservation, cultural tourism and other topics. This marks the third edition of the conference. The inaugural conference was held in November 2024 in Chengdu with the theme "Harmonious Coexistence Between Man and Nature." This year's event is co-hosted by the Brand Work Office of Xinhua News Agency, the agency's Sichuan branch, its news and information center, China Wildlife Conservation Association, China Conservation and Research Center for the Giant Panda, and Chengdu Media Group. Sichuan has the largest panda habitat in the world and is home to over 70 percent of China's wild giant panda population. Giant panda conservation serves as a microcosm of China's endeavors to advance ecological civilization. Thanks to sustained conservation efforts, the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2016 downgraded the giant panda's status from endangered to vulnerable. ■ This photo shows copies of a report centered on China's green development path, which is released during the main forum of the Global Panda Partners Conference 2026 in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province. item.title: New guardians carry forward age-old dialogue in China's Dunhuang
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
* The 9th Silk Road (Dunhuang) International Cultural Expo opened in Dunhuang on Tuesday, gathering around 1,200 delegates from home and abroad with a focus on cultural exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations. * Conservation technologies developed in Dunhuang have been rolled out to more than 150 heritage sites across China, and introduced to other countries including Kyrgyzstan and Myanmar. * While heritage guardians tend to Dunhuang's ancient roots, creative innovators breathe new life into its timeless culture. LANZHOU, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- Dunhuang, famed for its Mogao Caves, was a meeting place for diverse cultures along the ancient Silk Road. Today, it still draws people from far and wide, attracted by its renewed charm. The 9th Silk Road (Dunhuang) International Cultural Expo opened in Dunhuang on Tuesday, gathering around 1,200 delegates from home and abroad with a focus on cultural exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations. Yet the tales of cultural convergence stretch far beyond the expo's forums and exhibition halls, reaching into the daily rhythm of this oasis city, located in northwest China's Gansu Province. For many, Dunhuang is not merely a tourist attraction, but a second home where they build careers inspired by its age-old heritage. They, in turn, inject new energy into heritage preservation and cross-cultural exchange. Some foreign guests at the expo remarked after touring the city that Dunhuang itself stands as a living example of dialogue between different cultures. Zoey Ashlyn Koehl, a student from Oklahoma City University in the United States, was impressed by the welcoming and dynamic vibe of Dunhuang: "I think it's a city open to all different kinds of people to come." SAFEGUARDING HERITAGE Wu Shaoxia adjusted her equipment inside a cave as morning sunlight spilled over the cliff faces of the Mogao Caves. As a cultural relics photographer, she has been based in Dunhuang for 11 years. Now 35 and originally from Shaanxi Province, also in northwest China, Wu is part of the Dunhuang Academy's digital team, featuring many young members from across China. Wu regularly works inside the dim caves, repeating high-precision image capturing endeavors. Notably, she believes that "conservation is not only about rescuing endangered relics, but also racing against time to pass on the millennia-old beauty to future generations." The young cultural workers in Dunhuang carry forward a mission begun decades ago. Over 80 years ago, a batch of heritage workers trekked into the Gobi Desert in a grottoes' conservation and research quest. While their forerunners initially cleared sand from caves by hand and restored relics with simple tools, later generations have witnessed the evolution of conservation approaches. So far, the academy has completed high-precision digital documentation of 323 caves, while its online digital library reunites Dunhuang manuscripts scattered around the world. Notably, as part of the Mogao Caves visitor experience, a dome film that immerses viewers as if inside the real grottoes draws on the academy's digital records. Conservation technologies developed in Dunhuang have been rolled out to more than 150 heritage sites across China, and introduced to other countries including Kyrgyzstan and Myanmar. "Earlier generations safeguarded the physical grottoes. We strive to preserve the look of this 1,000-year-old treasure," said Wu. REIMAGINING TRADITIONS While heritage guardians tend to Dunhuang's ancient roots, creative innovators breathe new life into its timeless culture. Chen Lisong first visited Dunhuang ten years ago, instantly captivated by the depth of its ancient history. Previously based in Shanghai in east China, she relocated to Dunhuang the following year and opened a souvenir shop. The designs of her products draw on iconic Mogao motifs, including the nine-colored deer and flying apsaras. Chen later developed a Silk Road-themed dining space, where visitors can taste signature dishes from different regions along the ancient trade route. For her, Dunhuang culture is not limited to cave murals. It can be woven into dining, accommodation and travel experiences. "Through modern design, it can be transformed into items people can take home," she said. Shen Hongjie, a wood-carving artist, moved from central China's Hunan Province to Dunhuang in 2004, attracted by murals in the Mogao Caves and the local desert landscapes. He set up a studio, blending oil painting and traditional Chinese painting techniques with wood carving to recreate classic Mogao imagery. In the early years of his venture, Dunhuang's cultural tourism sector remained nascent, with limited sales channels for his artworks. As local cultural tourism flourished in recent years, more visitors have poured into Shen's studio, while young apprentices have traveled from afar to learn the craft. Dunhuang received some 24.39 million visitors in 2025, 3.7 times the number recorded in 2020. Cultural and creative products, immersive experiences and intangible heritage workshops are flourishing, appealing to culture-craving young Chinese. BRIDGING CONTINENTS Among those who fell for Dunhuang's charm are some cultural enthusiasts from overseas. Ukrainian dancer Romanovych Inna and Georgian dancer Vaja Bukia settled in Dunhuang in 2024, and have performed in the dance drama "Ancient Sound of Dunhuang." Discovering parallels between Georgian traditional dance and ancient Central Asian whirling dance movements depicted in Dunhuang's murals, Bukia incorporated his native dance elements into the show. "Both Georgia and Dunhuang carry ancient civilizations passed down for generations," he said. For American researcher Neil Schmid, the first full-time foreign scholar at the Dunhuang Academy, his connection with Dunhuang began in the 1980s after reading a book on it. He joined the academy in 2018 and has since shared Dunhuang's heritage globally via lectures, documentaries and publications. "The amazing thing about Dunhuang materials is that there is such a wealth," said Schmid. The ongoing Dunhuang expo, first launched in 2016, further expands such exchanges. Referring to the ancient legacy of Dunhuang, Daren Tang, director-general of the World Intellectual Property Organization, said at the expo: "It reminds us that culture does not grow in isolation, but through exchange, new ideas and creativity." Attending the expo for the second time, Hasebe Tsuyoshi, a professor from Japan's Kansai University who has been studying ancient Dunhuang music scores, said both the ancient and modern Dunhuang are crossroads of world cultures. "Different civilizations have interwoven with one another since ancient times," he said, adding that it is important to continue such exchange and interaction. (Video reporters: Zhang Zhimin and Zhao Tianlin; Video editors: Li Ziwei, Zhang Mocheng and Hong Liang) ■

item.title: Chinese premier calls for people-centered internet development amid AI advances
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-03
Chinese Premier Li Qiang delivers a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit in Wuzhen, east China's Zhejiang Province, Nov. 3, 2026. Li attended the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit and delivered a keynote speech here on Tuesday. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen) HANGZHOU, Nov. 3 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Tuesday called for a more people-centered approach to internet development amid rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI). Li made the remarks in a keynote speech delivered at the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit in Wuzhen, east China's Zhejiang Province, on Tuesday morning. Highlighting that the World Internet Conference has been held for 13 consecutive years, Li stressed that, despite rapid technological advances, one major question of common concern remains unchanged, namely how to make the internet better serve humanity. Li said the internet is undergoing an intelligent transformation and a systemic leap as it increasingly integrates with AI and other technologies. Stressing the need to place greater emphasis on a people-centered approach to internet development in today's world, Li said the ultimate purpose must be to promote the all-round development of people. He emphasized that internet-related technologies should enhance human capabilities, expand choices, affirm human value and improve well-being, rather than make humans subordinate to technology or exacerbate disparities in human development. Calling for joint efforts to build a community with a shared future in cyberspace, Li said China will continue to pursue innovation through openness, promote technology transfer and knowledge sharing, and work with other countries to foster an open, inclusive and dynamic digital innovation ecosystem. On digital security, Li said China will respect the legitimate cybersecurity concerns of all other countries and work together with them to address security challenges, while opposing the creation of a "digital iron curtain." Li also pledged that China will actively implement the Global Development Initiative and support Global South countries in building digital infrastructure and enhancing their digital technology capabilities. About 1,800 participants, including government officials, representatives of international organizations such as the United Nations and global internet companies, as well as experts and scholars, attended the opening ceremony. Following the opening, Li visited the Light of Internet Expo and Wuzhen's World Internet Science and Technology Museum. ■ Chinese Premier Li Qiang visits the Light of Internet Expo and Wuzhen's World Internet Science and Technology Museum following the opening of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit, in Wuzhen, east China's Zhejiang Province, Nov. 3, 2026. Li attended the opening ceremony of the 2026 World Internet Conference Wuzhen Summit and delivered a keynote speech here on Tuesday. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen)

item.title: Xi Focus: CPC charts course for tougher action against corruption, stronger self-governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-02
BEIJING, Nov. 2 (Xinhua) -- As China enters a critical period in its modernization drive, the ruling Communist Party of China (CPC) has charted the course for tougher action against corruption and stronger self-governance in the years ahead. Last week, the fifth plenary session of the 20th CPC Central Committee adopted a resolution on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance, underscoring the need to step up the fight against corruption and strengthen checks on and oversight over the exercise of power. In doing so, the CPC, the largest political party in the world with more than 100 million members, is seeking to overcome the unique challenges facing a party of its size. These challenges, as outlined by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, include how to maintain the Party's strong governance and leadership capacity, and sustain a clean and upright political environment. "It is now both imperative and timely for the Party to study issues concerning persevering with full and rigorous self-governance," Xi said in a January meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee that set the agenda of the plenum. IMPERATIVE THEME At the January meeting, Xi said the decision to focus the plenary session on Party self-governance had been made after thorough deliberation. Since it was founded in 1921, the Party has attached great importance to its self-supervision and self-governance. Today, the CPC's membership and ranks of officials have undergone structural changes, presenting new challenges for Party building. In response to these challenges, Xi has repeatedly stressed the need for an unwavering commitment to strict Party self-governance, sending a clear signal that discipline will be enforced ever more strictly. "It was with this in mind that the CPC Central Committee decided to make persevering with full and rigorous self-governance the plenum's agenda," he noted. Explaining the resolution at the plenary session, Xi emphasized that persevering with full and rigorous self-governance is essential for maintaining the Party's advanced nature and integrity and consolidating its long-term governing position. This year marks the beginning of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), a critical period for achieving the goal of basically realizing socialist modernization by 2035. "To successfully achieve the goals and tasks of the 15th Five-Year Plan, it is imperative to focus on enhancing the ability and competence of the Party in leading economic and social development," Xi told senior provincial- and ministerial-level officials attending a study session at the Party School of the CPC Central Committee earlier this year. HOW RESOLUTION TAKES SHAPE In January 2026, a drafting group was set up to prepare the resolution, with Xi at its helm. Throughout the drafting process, he played a decisive role, chairing multiple meetings, delivering important speeches and issuing instructions to guide the work. On Feb. 6, Xi chaired the group's first plenary meeting, where he outlined the key principles for the drafting of the resolution. He called for strict measures to address misconduct and corruption, while stressing that Party building should be pursued as a coordinated whole and integrated with the country's broader development goals. At the same meeting, Xi identified 39 key issues for further study, covering the full scope of Party building and governance. On May 6, Xi chaired a meeting in Shanghai on persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance, setting out further requirements for the drafting of the resolution. He called for a problem-oriented approach, stressing the need for firm action to tackle prominent problems. As the preparation of the document was underway, Xi stressed the importance of broad consultation and drawing on a wide range of views. He called on non-CPC parties and personages without party affiliation to speak candidly and offer constructive suggestions. During consultation on the draft resolution, 1,173 suggestions for revisions were received from localities, departments and various sectors. After careful consideration, the drafting group incorporated 208 suggestions. The document took shape over more than eight months, with the drafting group holding five plenary meetings and 35 specialized meetings. During the plenary session last week, participants held in-depth discussions and exchanged views, putting forward suggestions that led to 13 revisions to the draft resolution before it was finally adopted on Oct. 29. WHY RESOLUTION MATTERS The resolution examines new circumstances, challenges and tasks facing the Party as it advances full and rigorous Party self-governance. It identifies three increasingly arduous tasks for the CPC: safeguarding China's sovereignty, security and development interests amid a changing international environment; advancing reform and development while maintaining social harmony and stability at home; and preserving the Party's advanced nature and integrity. It also warns that, under new circumstances marked by profound changes, the Party faces challenges to its governance and leadership capacity, the quality of its membership, and its resistance against corruption and moral decline. The resolution has established a problem-oriented approach as one of the guiding principles for persevering with full and rigorous Party self-governance. It places particular emphasis on strengthening Party spirit among CPC members, as problems in Party conduct and discipline often stem from a lack of strong Party spirit. The resolution sets out specific measures to ensure that Party members and officials remain loyal, upright, and responsible. Another focus is eliminating hidden rules and curbing malpractices such as cultivating connections and making back-room deals. The resolution sets out concrete measures to root out such practices. The more than 200 measures outlined in the resolution combine the reinforcement of existing requirements with new responses to emerging challenges. In the fight against corruption, for example, the resolution calls for intensified efforts to expose new and concealed forms of graft. These include the use of proxies, or so-called "white gloves," to disguise illicit dealings, as well as the "revolving door" phenomenon of bureaucrat-merchant collusion after officials' retirement. It also calls for a crackdown on corruption involving the internet, virtual currencies, cross-border capital flows and blockchain technology. The resolution also sets out measures to improve the Party and state oversight systems and ensure that political responsibility for full and rigorous Party self-governance is effectively discharged. "No other political party in the world takes its own development as seriously as the CPC does, or advances its own self-reform with such a high degree of self-awareness, scientific rigor and systematic effort," Xi has said. "This is a distinctive strength of our Party." The resolution, as observers point out, signals a renewed commitment by the CPC to advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance with higher standards and more concrete measures, recognizing this as a fundamental underpinning of the broader endeavor to build China into a strong country and advance national rejuvenation. "We have already forged a bright path ahead, and we must keep moving forward," Xi has said. ■
